narrative.en: Unpen-ji comes 20.5 km in, and nothing is mapped in the 10.0 km before it. The map gives it a height of 911 m, the highest of the seven it gives this section's temples; the other sixteen carry none. A viewpoint and a café stand just past it. Daikō-ji follows 321 m past the 30 km edge of the band the day cut ends days in, so no temple ends this day and it runs on to Fujikawa Ryokan. Fourteen bus stops stand on it, and nothing on it is mapped as a town.

reflection.en: Daikō-ji stands three hundred and twenty-one metres past where a day of this length would have ended. How much of a day is decided by three hundred metres?

end.note: Temple 76, 67.62 km along this section's walked line, 15 m off it — 29.33 km from the previous day's end at 38.29 km, inside the 25-30 km band and, of the temples in it, the one nearest 27.5 km.

theme.en: Nine temples, and a hundred and seventeen metres between the first two

narrative.en: More temples stand on this day than on any other of the six. It begins on a pair: Jinne-in 0.8 km in and Kannon-ji 117 m after it, the narrowest step between temples in this section. Motoyama-ji follows, and then the spacing opens — 11.7 km to Iyadani-ji, with 6.6 km inside it holding nothing mapped at all, ending at Mitoyo. Five more temples come in the 11.9 km after Iyadani-ji, two of them, Mandara-ji and Shusshaka-ji, 0.46 km apart. Three more places meet the way at exactly the point Zentsū-ji does — a sacred place, a wayside shrine and a place to stay — and Konzō-ji closes the day.

reflection.en: The closest two temples in this section stand on this day, and so does its emptiest stretch. Does a day have one shape, or as many as you notice?

theme.en: Four towns in eleven kilometres, and then none for sixty

narrative.en: Four of Sanuki's mapped towns stand on this one day, inside 11.4 km of each other — Tadotsu, Marugame, Utazu and Sakaide, where the day ends. It is the shortest of the six, and the day after it is the longest of the forty. More places stand on it to the kilometre than on any other day here, thirty of them places to eat. Dōryū-ji comes 4.0 km in and Goshō-ji 11.2. No temple falls where a day of this length would end — Sanuki Kokubun-ji falls just short of the band and Shiromine-ji just past it — so the day stops at a town instead, and the next place the map could have stopped it is 59.6 km on.

reflection.en: The shortest day of the six stands directly before the longest, and one gap in the map makes both. Does a map owe you an even pace?

end.note: OpenStreetMap node/1012320229 (town), 142.09 km along this section's walked line, 172 m off it. No temple falls 25-30 km past the previous day's end at 82.48 km, so the day ends at the named accommodation or town waypoint on the line nearest 27.5 km, 59.61 km on.

warnings.en: 59.6 km, the longest day on the circuit. OpenStreetMap records no named accommodation or town on the walked line between Sakaide and Sanuki, so the rule had nowhere nearer to stop. Carry water and food for the whole distance, or break the day at a place off the line.

theme.en: The longest day of the forty, and the most crowded

narrative.en: 59.6 km, the longest day of the forty this cut made, and it is long for an absence: nothing is mapped as a place to stay for 86.1 km, and this day is 59.6 of that stretch. No town falls in it either, until the one it ends at. What the day is not is empty. More places stand on this one day than on any other of the six, and the longest run with nothing mapped on it is only 4.2 km. Seven temples come among them — Tennō-ji, Sanuki Kokubun-ji, Shiromine-ji, Negoro-ji, Ichinomiya-ji, Yashima-ji and Yakuri-ji — and thirty-one places to eat. Everything except somewhere to stop.

reflection.en: The busiest day in Sanuki and the longest of the forty, and those are one fact: nothing mapped on it is a place to sleep. How much of what you carry is decided by what someone wrote down?

end.note: Temple 88, 162.43 km along this section's walked line, 19 m off it — 20.34 km from the previous day's end at 142.09 km. Held fixed rather than chosen: the temple sequence completes here, and what follows is the circuit's closing return to Temple 1.

theme.en: The last three of the eighty-eight

narrative.en: Shidō-ji stands 0.7 km into this day, Nagao-ji 7.6, and Ōkubo-ji closes it — the eighty-sixth, eighty-seventh and eighty-eighth temples. The last mapped places to stay before Ōkubo-ji come 8 km in, and of the 12.7 km from Nagao-ji to Ōkubo-ji, 8.7 carry nothing mapped at all. Neither arm of the day cut chose this ending — Ōkubo-ji is held, because the temple sequence completes there.

reflection.en: The numbering ends at this day's last temple, and the walking has 39.8 km left. Which of the two were you counting?

theme.en: From the eighty-eighth to the first

narrative.en: A temple stands at each end of this day and none between them: Ōkubo-ji, the eighty-eighth, and Ryōzen-ji, the first. 39.8 km, the second-longest of Sanuki's days, and fewer places are mapped on it than on any other day here. Minshuku Yasokubo comes 0.2 km in, and past Ōkubo-ji nothing else is mapped as a place to stay or a town. After it 24.7 km carry nothing mapped at all, the longest such stretch in this section. Then a station, a shrine and a shop inside 1.1 km, then 12.6 km more with a single vending machine on them. The last thing mapped is a bus stop 76 m short of the end, named for the temple it stands in front of. Ryōzen-ji closes Sanuki, and Awa's first day starts from the same point.

reflection.en: Every other section ends where the next one begins; this one ends where the first one began. Who decides when a walk is finished?
